newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadians decide on Chretien's record.
newsitem.headline: Canadians decide on Chretien's record.

text.p: Canadians voted on Monday in a general election that pollsters say could give budget-slashing Prime Minister Jean Chretien's ruling Liberal Party a new but reduced mandate.

The sun shone across much of the country as the population went to the polls to chose a new House of Commons. But clouds or rain were predicted for a few cities and, in true Canadian fashion, snow flurries were possible in the Atlantic region of Labrador.

Chretien's Liberals maintained a substantial lead over the other four main parties in polls before the weekend but analysts said they could suffer a reduced majority or possibly even a minority of the 301 seats.

"I think it was great to vote, it's a great day, a beautiful day, and I'm very confident," Chretien said after voting in a small primary school in Ste.-Flore, a Quebec hamlet near his birthplace northeast of Montreal.

Looking relaxed and wearing a suit, Chretien shook many villagers' hands before taking the rest of the day off, while his accompanying press corps went off to a tournament he organized at a golf course he used to own.

Chretien, who became the first prime minister since the 1960s to successfully attack Canada's budget deficits, had called the election 1-1/2 years before constitutionally necessary because of his strong lead in the polls.
But a combination of attacks from his four main rivals and what analysts call a campaign without an imperative has cut into his margin.

He had swept the Conservatives out of power in 1993 with 177 of 295 seats. But polls indicated a failure to expand his weak base in the West suggested that the Conservatives could crack his grip on the maritime provinces in the East.
His opponents attacked his government's handling of unemployment which during his entire mandate was stuck stubbornly above the nine percent rate.
Vying for the right-wing vote, the Conservative and Reform parties called for tax cuts while on the left the New Democrats suggested stimulative spending.

Polls suggested the western-based Reform -- which takes a tough-love approach on Quebec secessionists -- would win the second highest number of seats and replace the separatist Bloc Quebecois as the official opposition.
A steady stream of mostly older Canadians entered a gym in a public school in bright morning sunshine in downtown Ottawa.
One voter, Dr. John Slauson, said he voted against the Liberals "to keep them honest" but most of his friends would not be going to the polls.
"They don't seem to be very interested in it. There's not much enthusiasm," he said. "People who are politically active are really active. Everyone else is sleeping."
In contrast to the United States, where many stations have machines with levers that voters press, all Canadian voting is done on paper ballots.

And there is only one choice -- which member of Parliament do you want -- rather than the sometimes bewildering menu of choices from president down to town alderman, along with possible referendum questions, in the United States.

One of the defining issues that emerged in this 36-day campaign was how to deal with French-speaking Quebec -- whether to promote reconciliation, however vaguely defined, or to stand up to separatists even if this might enflame them.
Reform capitalized on the fact that many Canadians are sick of the debate and tired of Quebec demands, scaring others however who worried that it might renew the secessionists.

Chretien also stirred the pot, apparently driving some wavering Quebeckers to the separatist camp, by declaring he would not recognize a simple majority of voters in a future referendum on Quebec independence.
For the Conservatives, which have alternated with the Liberals in running Canada since its confederation in 1867, the election was crucial.
The Conservatives were reduced to just two seats in the 1993 election, and if they fail to make a good recovery this time people will be questioning their survival as a national party.

Some on the right have called for Reform and the Conservatives to join forces and stop splitting the vote, but enough bad blood has been spilled between the leaders of the two parties that this seemed difficult for now at least. Conservative leader Jean Charest ruled it out on the weekend.
Polls were closing at 7 p.m. EDT (1100 GMT) in Newfoundland, and 2-1/2 hours later in most of the rest of the country, with all polls shut by 10:30 p.m. EDT (0230 GMT Tuesday).
